topComments.author: skydhash
topComments.text: Was initially interested (I like languages that binds easily to C because of the nice libraries there, and I'm a fan of LISP), but the README is LLM-generated and the Makefile is unreadable. The there's this part in the AI policy It is simply not feasible for humans to keep the entirety of large projects in their heads all at once. When working on a project, one is constantly forgetting and relearning code along the way. The situation is even worse for projects where multiple people work together and no one knows what everyone else was thinking. We look at the code and try to build up sufficient context in our heads to make the necessary changes. When we misjudge that context or misunderstand existing code, we end up making mistakes. It's a made up excuse because no one has ever tried doing that. Instead the core activity of software engineering (and engineering in general) is to break down things into modular components, ensure that they work well, produce specs, then assemble the result. Which is why no one read the source code for open(2) system call before using it. Instead they read the manpage and only when there's an issue there's a need to compare the specs with the implementation. So it's a matter of communication between humans. If person A is responsible for module 1 and person B's module 2 depends on the former. It's up to A to provide a proper spec to B. It's not up to B to learn everything about module 1's implementation and doing so is kinda foolish. So something like Any new code that is added is therefore always done with limited understanding. Is a red flag. The codebase and workflow should be that new additions should deal with a limited context (as in one PR shouldn't touch unrelated things) at at time and the contributors should be able to come with a full understanding of what they are doing. If they cannot, it's either a failure of the codebase, the docs, the workflows, or the contributors.

stories.title: A 512 KiB binary message teaching chess without a shared language
stories.author: legotin

topComments.author: legotin
topComments.text: I built Golden Board, a 512 KiB binary message designed to teach chess to an unknown recipient without shared language, culture, or prior knowledge of the game. The project is inspired by a tradition of messages designed for an unknown intelligence such as Voyager Golden Record, Lincos and others. But instead of sharing science or art, it teaches chess. Why chess? Because a small set of rules opens up an enormous world of ideas and beauty. We can teach it from scratch and then let the recipient explore a rich legacy shaped by centuries of human ingenuity, sacrifices, and moments of brilliance. The message begins by teaching the recipient to count, recognize bytes, and gradually decode and understand everything that follows. I tested it extensively, using LLMs to simulate an unknown recipient and carefully checking each part of the message. Of course, LLMs are far from perfect stand-ins, but those experiments helped me identify ambiguities and improve the design. The project is an attempt to solve a broader problem: its bootstrap is chess-agnostic and designed to decode other structured messages. Anyone is welcome to build on it and create messages that teach something entirely different. Source code and docs: https://github.com/arlegotin/golden-board

stackOverflowQuestions.title: should I avoid std::optional<const T>, similarly to std::vector<const T>?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: const in C++ is not so simple to use and reason about when it comes to composite types. Many realize this fact when considering std::vector : non-const vectors of const elements vs. const vector of non-const elements: How can I specify a vector parameter so that values may change but the vector structure won't? const vector implies const elements? Now, what about std::optional ? If we use a std::optional<const T> , we can clear or replace the value of T - without changing the existing value, as constructing and destructing const T is quite legitimate. So, the const 'ness is somewhat arbitrary. Should we, therefore, avoid the "circumventable" constness of types within optional 's, and just stick to the non-const value types, like we do with std::vector 's? See also: Is the content of a const std::optional always const?

infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data
infoqArticles.description: Airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search. The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available. By Robert Krzaczyński
infoqArticles.author: Robert Krzaczyński

infoqArticles.title: Article: Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility

infoqArticles.author: Purnang Borah

infoqArticles.author: Daniel Dominguez

infoqArticles.title: GitHub Rebuilds the Copilot App's Diff Surface to Open Million-Line Pull Requests Without Jank
